summary.title: Why I Think You Should Almost Never Use AI to Write Anything Substantive
summary.one_liner: Writing is part of thinking, and AI-written prose is vague and subtly wrong in ways that are hard to notice, so using it for substantive writing (even when edited) is usually a bad trade and can mislead readers unless clearly labeled.
takeaways: The writing process is part of the research and thinking process; drafting prose forces you to find holes in your argument.
AI-written text tends to be vague, dense with empty phrases, and wrong in subtle, convincing ways that take real effort to spot.
Using AI for brainstorming, transcription, analysis, feedback, and line editing is considered acceptable; using it to write the substance is the concern.
Publishing AI-written text without labeling it breaks the implicit contract with readers; labeled, clearly marked AI output is more acceptable.
The author illustrates the problems with a worked critique of a Claude-generated paragraph on AI chip smuggling.
summary.summary: This is a personal essay arguing that people should almost never use AI to write substantive text, even with detailed notes or after editing. The author gives three reasons: writing is part of thinking, AI prose is vague and wrong in hard-to-notice ways, and undisclosed AI writing is rude and misleading to readers. The essay quotes Paul Graham, Clara Collier, Patrick McKenzie, and Eric Schwitzgebel, and works through a line-by-line critique of a Claude-generated paragraph on AI chip smuggling. It closes with a Q&A on exceptions such as labeled AI quotes, translation, formulaic emails, and high-stakes policy writing.
